claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 is a high-entropy alloy with a reported hierarchical heterostructure.
A machine-learning surrogate trained on high-fidelity microstructural descriptors and test data can predict Young's modulus in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
A machine-learning surrogate trained on high-fidelity microstructural descriptors and test data can predict yield strength in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
A machine-learning surrogate trained on high-fidelity microstructural descriptors and test data can predict fracture toughness in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed surrogate will predict the target properties more accurately than established simulation methods.
The proposed surrogate will predict the target properties faster than established simulation methods.
Nanoprecipitate morphology mediates deformation and fracture in the target hierarchical alloy.
Interface characteristics mediate deformation and fracture in the target hierarchical alloy.
The interplay of lattice distortion, nanoprecipitation, and interface mechanics has quantifiable effects on macroscopic mechanical response.
Mapping detailed structural descriptors directly to macroscopic properties can bypass part of the computational burden of traditional simulations.
The surrogate is expected to improve RMSE by approximately 10–15% relative to conventional simulation methods.
The surrogate will enable near-real-time property estimation.
Conventional atomistic simulation methods require long computation times.
Conventional continuum and atomistic methods often struggle to capture multiscale interactions in hierarchical heterostructures.
Failure to measure critical microstructural descriptors could prevent accurate prediction of mechanical behavior.
Excessive sample-to-sample microstructural variability could impair model generalization.
Processing artifacts could decouple measured structure from mechanical performance and cause model failure.
Predictive gains may vary with experimental noise and processing consistency.
Prediction deviations greater than 20% across multiple independent samples, or failure to improve computational efficiency, are predeclared as falsifying outcomes.
